parts.label: (a)

markscheme_points.text: sum of CW moments = sum of ACW moments
about the same point for (an object in rotational) equilibrium

hints: Hint 1: Think about a see-saw or balance that is perfectly still and not starting to turn - what must be true about the turning effects trying to rotate it each way?
Hint 2: Remember to compare clockwise moments with anticlockwise moments taken about the same pivot, and link this to rotational equilibrium.
parts.proper_answer: For a body in rotational equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about the same point.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What equilibrium means for turning**
Imagine holding a ruler at a pivot. If it stays still and does not start to rotate, the total tendency to turn clockwise must exactly cancel the total tendency to turn anticlockwise. That is rotational equilibrium.

Step 2: **State the principle fully**
So you can say: $$ \text{sum of clockwise moments} = \text{sum of anticlockwise moments} $$ This is only true when both sides are calculated about the same point and the object is in rotational equilibrium.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
A hollow plastic sphere is attached at one end of a bar. The sphere is partially submerged in water and the bar is attached to a fixed vertical support by a pivot P, as shown in Fig. 3.1.

{{figure:figure_3_1}}

Fig. 3.1 (not to scale)

The sphere has weight $0.30\,\text{N}$. The distance from P to the centre of gravity of the sphere is $0.29\,\text{m}$. Assume that the weight of the bar is negligible.

Calculate the moment of the weight of the sphere about P.
hints: Hint 1: The weight of the sphere acts straight down, but the 0.29 m bar is tilted at 40 degrees to the horizontal - look for the horizontal distance from P to the line of action of the weight.
Hint 2: Use moment = force x perpendicular distance from P, which here becomes $0.30 \times 0.29 \cos 40^{\circ}$, then calculate in N m.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Perpendicular distance is the key**
A moment is force times the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force: $$ \text{moment} = F \times d_{\perp} $$ Here $F = 0.30\text{ N}$ weight acts vertically down at the centre of the sphere.

Step 2: **Find the horizontal arm**
From Fig. 3.1 the distance along the bar is $0.29\text{ m}$ at $40^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. The perpendicular (horizontal) distance from P to the vertical weight line is: $$ d_{\perp} = 0.29 \cos 40^{\circ} \approx 0.222\text{ m} $$

Step 3: **Calculate the moment**
$$ \text{moment} = 0.30 \times 0.29 \cos 40^{\circ} $$ $$ \text{moment} \approx 0.067\text{ N m} $$ This is a clockwise moment about P due to the weight.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem:
The system shown in Fig. 3.1 is part of a mechanism that controls the amount of water in a tank.

Water enters the tank and causes the sphere to rise. This results in the bar becoming horizontal. Fig. 3.2 shows the system in its new position.

{{figure:figure_3_2}}

Fig. 3.2 (not to scale)

In this position the rod R exerts a force to compress a horizontal spring that controls the water supply to the tank. R is positioned at a perpendicular distance of $0.017\,\text{m}$ above P.

The variation of the force $F$ applied to the spring with compression $x$ of the spring is shown in Fig. 3.3.

{{figure:figure_3_3}}

Fig. 3.3
parts.text: Use Fig. 3.3 to calculate the spring constant $k$ of the spring.

markscheme_points.text: k = F / x or k = gradient

hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 3.3 - force F is proportional to compression x, so the graph is a straight line through the origin. What does the steepness of that line tell you about the stiffness?
Hint 2: Pick a large, easy point on the line, convert x from mm to m, then use $k = F/x$ to find k in N m^{-1}.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Stiffness from the graph**
For a spring obeying Hooke's law: $$ F = kx $$ So $k$ is the gradient of the $F$ against $x$ graph. A steeper line means a stiffer spring.

Step 2: **Read values and convert units**
Take a point far along the line for accuracy, for example $F = 21\text{ N}$ at $x = 10\text{ mm} = 10 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}$. Then: $$ k = \frac{F}{x} = \frac{21}{10 \times 10^{-3}} $$ $$ k = 2100\text{ N m}^{-1} $$ Any other point on the line gives the same result.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.part_stem:
At the position shown in Fig. 3.2, the system is stationary and in equilibrium.

The radius of the sphere is $0.0480\,\text{m}$ and $26.0\%$ of the volume of the sphere is submerged.
The density of water is $1.00 \times 10^3\,\text{kg}\,\text{m}^{-3}$.
parts.text: Show that the upthrust on the sphere is $1.18\,\text{N}$.
hints: Hint 1: Upthrust equals the weight of water displaced, so start by finding the full volume of the spherical shell from its radius, then take only the submerged fraction.
Hint 2: Use $V = 4/3 \pi r^3$ with $r = 0.0480$ m, multiply by 0.26 for the submerged volume, then use $\text{upthrust} = \rho g V_{submerged}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Full volume of sphere**
The sphere displaces water equal to its submerged volume. First find the total volume: $$ V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \frac{4}{3}\pi (0.0480)^3 $$ This gives $V \approx 4.63 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^3$.

Step 2: **Weight of displaced water**
Only $26.0\%$ is submerged: $$ V_{sub} = 0.260 V $$ Upthrust is the weight of this water: $$ \text{upthrust} = \rho g V_{sub} = 1000 \times 9.81 \times V \times 0.260 $$ $$ \text{upthrust} \approx 1.18\text{ N} $$ acting vertically upwards on the sphere.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.text: By taking moments about P, determine the force exerted on the spring by the rod R.
hints: Hint 1: In Fig. 3.2 the bar is horizontal and balanced, so focus on all vertical forces at 0.29 m from P and the horizontal spring force at 0.017 m above P - which way does each tend to turn the bar?
Hint 2: Set anticlockwise moment from upthrust equal to clockwise moments from weight plus spring force: $1.18 \times 0.29 = 0.30 \times 0.29 + F \times 0.017$, then solve for F.
parts.proper_answer: Taking moments about P: $(1.18 \times 0.29) = (0.30 \times 0.29) + (F \times 0.017)$, giving $F = 15 \text{ N}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify the three moments about P**
With the bar horizontal, both weight ($0.30\text{ N}$ down) and upthrust ($1.18\text{ N}$ up) act at $0.29\text{ m}$ from P. Upthrust tries to rotate the bar anticlockwise, weight tries to rotate it clockwise. The spring pushes on rod R with force $F$ at perpendicular distance $0.017\text{ m}$ above P, also giving a clockwise moment.

Step 2: **Apply balance of moments**
For equilibrium: $$ \text{anticlockwise moment} = \text{clockwise moments} $$ $$ 1.18 \times 0.29 = 0.30 \times 0.29 + F \times 0.017 $$

Step 3: **Solve for F**
$$ F = \frac{(1.18-0.30)\times 0.29}{0.017} $$ $$ F \approx 15\text{ N} $$ This is the force exerted on the spring by rod R.

parts.label: (c)(iv)
parts.text: Calculate the elastic potential energy $E_{\text{p}}$ of the compressed spring.
hints: Hint 1: The spring now stores elastic energy - think how energy depends on both the force you found and how far the spring is squashed, which you can get from your k value.
Hint 2: First find compression $x = F/k = 15/2100$, then use $E_P = 1/2 Fx$ or $1/2 kx^2$ to get energy in joules.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Energy in a stretched or compressed spring**
Work done to compress the spring is stored as elastic potential energy: $$ E_P = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 = \frac{1}{2}Fx $$ where $x$ is compression and $F = kx$.

Step 2: **Find compression then energy**
From (c)(i) $k = 2100\text{ N m}^{-1}$ and from (c)(iii) $F = 15\text{ N}$: $$ x = \frac{F}{k} = \frac{15}{2100} \approx 7.14 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m} $$ Then: $$ E_P = \frac{1}{2} \times 15 \times \frac{15}{2100} \approx 0.054\text{ J} $$ You can also read $x \approx 7.1\text{ mm}$ directly from Fig. 3.3 for $F = 15\text{ N}$.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text:
When the sphere moves from the position shown in Fig. 3.1 to the position shown in Fig. 3.2, the upthrust on the sphere does work.
Assume that resistive forces are negligible.

Explain why the work done by the upthrust is not equal to the gain in elastic potential energy of the spring.

markscheme_points.text: the sphere has gained gravitational potential energy

hints: Hint 1: Track where the energy from the work done by upthrust goes as the sphere rises from the lower tilted position to the higher horizontal position.
parts.proper_answer: The sphere rises so gains gravitational potential energy, so not all the work done by upthrust is transferred to elastic potential energy of the spring.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Energy is shared, not just stored in the spring**
As water rises the sphere moves up from Fig. 3.1 to Fig. 3.2. Work done by the upward upthrust force lifts the weight of the sphere, so the sphere gains gravitational potential energy $mgh$. Only the remainder of the work appears as elastic potential energy in the spring, so the two quantities are not equal.
